title: Figma's Prototyping Model — Hotspot, Connection, Destination
content:
Every Figma prototype reduces to one primitive: an INTERACTION attached to a layer. An interaction has three parts.

1. TRIGGER — what the user does (On click, On drag, Mouse enter, After delay...).
2. ACTION — what happens (Navigate to, Change to, Open overlay, Set variable, Conditional...).
3. ANIMATION — how it happens (Instant, Dissolve, Smart animate, Move in, Push, Slide in) plus easing and duration.

The layer carrying the interaction is the HOTSPOT. The line drawn to the target is the CONNECTION. The target is the DESTINATION.

HARD RULES:
- Navigation destinations must be TOP-LEVEL FRAMES (direct children of the page). You cannot navigate to a nested frame or a group.
- Any layer can be a hotspot — frame, group, text, shape, instance.
- A single trigger can carry an unlimited stack of actions (Multiple actions), executed top to bottom.
- Interactions live in the Prototype tab of the right sidebar; the Design tab has none of this.

MENTAL MODEL: treat a Figma prototype as a state machine where frames are states, connections are transitions, and variables are the state you cannot express as a frame. The moment you find yourself duplicating frames to represent data, switch to variables.
source: help.figma.com — Guide to prototyping in Figma

title: Flows and Starting Points — Structuring a Prototype
content:
A FLOW is a named entry point into your prototype. The STARTING POINT is the first frame of that flow.

MECHANICS:
- Figma auto-creates a flow starting point the first time you connect two frames.
- Add more: select the frame → Prototype tab → 'Flow starting point' → +. Or right-click the frame → 'Add starting point'.
- Each flow gets a name and an optional description; both appear in Presentation view's flow menu and in the share link.
- One file can hold many flows. Each is independently playable and independently shareable.

HOW TO STRUCTURE THEM:
- One flow per user task, not per screen group. 'Checkout — guest', 'Checkout — returning', 'Wallet connect — first time'.
- Name flows the way a stakeholder would search for them, not the way your file is organised.
- Write the description as the test task: 'You want to buy the blue variant in size M and pay with Shop Pay.' The description becomes the usability-test script.
- Keep a 'Sandbox' page with no starting points for exploration, so half-built screens never show up in a share link.

ANTI-PATTERN: one giant flow covering the whole product. Stakeholders get lost, testers wander, and you cannot answer a single research question cleanly.
source: help.figma.com — Prototype flows and starting points

title: Complete Trigger Reference — All 12 Figma Prototype Triggers
content:
POINTER AND TOUCH
- On click / On tap — click on desktop, tap on mobile. The default and the one to reach for 90% of the time.
- Mouse enter — fires the moment the cursor enters the hotspot. Does NOT revert on exit.
- Mouse leave — fires the moment the cursor leaves the hotspot.
- Mouse down (touch down) — fires on press, before release.
- Mouse up (touch up) — fires on release.
- While hovering — fires on enter and REVERTS to the original frame on exit. Figma explicitly recommends Mouse enter + Mouse leave instead, because the revert is not configurable.
- While pressing — fires on press-and-hold and REVERTS on release. Good for a genuine :active state.
- On drag — fires when the hotspot is dragged. Direction options: Left, Right, Up, Down. Drag is bidirectional — the user can drag back through the transition, which makes it the only trigger with a scrubbable feel.

TIME
- After delay — fires after N milliseconds on the frame. Set the duration explicitly. Used for splash screens, auto-advancing carousels, toast auto-dismiss, and simulated loading.

INPUT DEVICE
- Keyboard / Gamepad — bind a single key or a key combination. Officially supported controllers: Xbox One, PS4, Nintendo Switch Pro.

VIDEO
- When video hits — fires at a timestamp. A timestamp past the video length fires at the end.
- When video ends — fires on completion.

title: Choosing the Right Trigger — Decision Rules
content:
USE MOUSE ENTER + MOUSE LEAVE, NOT WHILE HOVERING. While hovering hard-codes an instant revert you cannot animate. Enter/leave gives you two independent interactions, each with its own animation and duration, so a dropdown can ease open in 200ms and ease closed in 150ms.

USE WHILE PRESSING FOR :ACTIVE. It is the only trigger that reverts on release, which is exactly what a pressed button state is. Mouse down + Mouse up is the fallback when you need the press to persist.

USE MOUSE DOWN WHEN LATENCY MATTERS. On a keypad, a swatch picker, or a trading interface, firing on down feels instant; firing on click feels laggy. Never use Mouse down for destructive actions — the user loses the ability to abort by dragging off.

USE ON DRAG FOR ANYTHING WITH A PHYSICAL METAPHOR. Bottom sheets, carousels, swipe-to-delete, sliders, pull-to-refresh. Because drag is bidirectional and scrubbable, it is the only trigger that communicates 'this thing follows my finger'.

USE AFTER DELAY SPARINGLY. It is the right tool for auto-dismiss and simulated latency and the wrong tool for anything the user should control. A 3000ms delay in a usability test reads as a bug, not a feature.

DO NOT SIMULATE TAB ORDER WITH KEYBOARD TRIGGERS unless you are specifically testing keyboard navigation — it is a lot of wiring for a result that Dev Mode annotations communicate better.

ON MOBILE PROTOTYPES: hover triggers do not exist. Any interaction that only appears on hover is invisible on touch. If your prototype needs Mouse enter to reveal an action, you have found a real affordance bug, not a prototyping limitation.

title: Complete Action Reference — All 15 Figma Prototype Actions
content:
NAVIGATION
- Navigate to — go to a top-level frame. Adds to prototype history.
- Back — return to the previous frame in history.
- Open link — open an external URL in a new tab.
- Scroll to — scroll the current frame to any object inside it. Options: Instant or animated (with easing and duration).

COMPONENT STATE
- Change to — switch the current component instance to another variant in the same component set. This is the interactive-components action.

OVERLAYS
- Open overlay — render the destination frame above the current frame.
- Close overlay — dismiss the topmost overlay.
- Swap overlay — replace the current overlay with another. Does NOT add to history, so Back skips it.

DATA AND LOGIC
- Set variable — assign a new value to a variable. The 'to:' field accepts an expression.
- Set variable mode — switch the variable mode of the page mid-prototype (theme switching, locale switching, density switching).
- Conditional — evaluate an if/else boolean expression and run nested actions per branch.

VIDEO
- Play / pause video — play, pause, or toggle.
- Mute / unmute video — mute, unmute, or toggle.
- Set to specific time — jump to a timestamp.
- Jump forward / backward in time — seek by N seconds.

MULTIPLE ACTIONS: any trigger can stack an unlimited number of these, run in listed order. The canonical pattern is Set variable → Conditional → Navigate to, so state updates before the branch is evaluated.

title: Navigate To vs Change To — The Most Consequential Choice
content:
These two actions look interchangeable and are not. Choosing wrong is the single biggest cause of unmaintainable Figma prototypes.

NAVIGATE TO moves between top-level frames. The whole screen is replaced. Use it when the URL would change in production, when the page-level context changes, or when you genuinely want a new screen in prototype history so Back works.

CHANGE TO swaps a variant inside a component set, in place. Nothing else on the screen moves. Use it for any state that lives inside a component: button hover/pressed, checkbox on/off, accordion open/closed, tab selected, toggle, input focus, card expanded.

THE MATH THAT SETTLES IT: a form with five checkboxes prototyped with Navigate to needs 2^5 = 32 frames and roughly 160 connections. Prototyped with Change to on a single interactive checkbox component, it needs one frame and two interactions total. Figma's own documentation uses this exact example.

RULE OF THUMB: if the change is smaller than the screen, it is Change to. If the change IS the screen, it is Navigate to.

CONSEQUENCE FOR HANDOFF: Change to maps to a component prop in code. Navigate to maps to a route. Getting this right in Figma means your prototype's structure already matches the engineer's component tree — which is why this decision is a handoff decision, not just a prototyping one.

title: Prototype History, Back, and Swap Overlay
content:
Figma maintains a linear history stack of frames visited via Navigate to and overlays opened via Open overlay. The Back action pops the stack.

WHAT ENTERS HISTORY: Navigate to, Open overlay.
WHAT DOES NOT: Swap overlay, Change to, Set variable, Scroll to.

WHY SWAP OVERLAY MATTERS: in a multi-step modal (a 3-step wallet connect, a variant picker, a KYC step flow) use Swap overlay between steps. Because swaps do not enter history, a single Back or Close overlay returns the user to the underlying page rather than stepping backwards through modal steps one at a time. If you want step-by-step back-navigation inside a modal, use Open overlay for each step instead and accept the stack.

COMMON BUG: chaining Open overlay repeatedly inside a modal flow. Overlays stack on top of each other, dim backgrounds multiply, and Close overlay only dismisses the top one. The user ends up trapped behind three layers of scrim. Use Swap overlay.

BACK ON THE FIRST FRAME does nothing — there is no history. If a flow's first frame has a back arrow, either wire it to a plausible parent screen with Navigate to or remove it, because in a usability test a dead back button reads as a broken product.

title: Overlays — Positions, Backgrounds, and Dismissal
content:
Open overlay renders a frame ABOVE the current frame without leaving it. The current frame stays live underneath, keeps its scroll position, and keeps its state.

POSITION: seven presets — Top left, Top centre, Top right, Centre, Bottom left, Bottom centre, Bottom right — plus Manual, which lets you drag the overlay to an exact offset. Manual is what you use for tooltips and popovers anchored to a specific control.

CLOSE WHEN CLICKING OUTSIDE: a checkbox. Adds click-outside-to-dismiss without any extra hotspot. Turn it ON for non-blocking overlays (dropdowns, popovers, tooltips, filter panels). Turn it OFF for anything requiring an explicit decision (destructive confirmation, transaction signing, terms acceptance) — dismissing a 'Confirm swap' modal by clicking the page is a real-money bug in crypto UI.

ADD BACKGROUND BEHIND OVERLAY: a colour + opacity behind the overlay and in front of the current frame. This is your scrim. Match it to your token (commonly black at 40–60%). Turn it OFF for popovers and dropdowns — a scrim on a dropdown reads as a modal and blocks perceived interaction with the page.

TRANSITION ANIMATION: overlays accept Instant, Dissolve, Move in, Slide in — but NOT Smart animate directly. You can, however, use Smart animate when SWAPPING between overlays that share matching layers, which is how you build a multi-step modal whose header morphs between steps.

FIXED POSITION IN OVERLAYS: an overlay can itself contain a scrolling body plus fixed header and footer, which is how you build a scrollable bottom sheet with a pinned CTA.
source: help.figma.com — Create overlays in your prototypes

title: Overlay or Navigate? A Decision Rule
content:
USE AN OVERLAY when the underlying context must survive. The user should feel they never left the page: filter panels, quick-view, cart drawer, confirmation dialogs, tooltips, date pickers, transaction confirmation, image lightbox.

USE NAVIGATE TO when the context is genuinely replaced: a new page, a full-screen takeover, a distinct step in a linear funnel with its own URL.

THE PRODUCTION TEST: ask 'would this have its own URL?' If yes, Navigate to. If no, overlay. This keeps your prototype's structure isomorphic to the routing an engineer will build.

THE STATE TEST: ask 'if the user dismisses this, should the page be exactly as they left it — same scroll, same filters, same form input?' If yes, overlay. Navigate to + Back can preserve scroll (see Preserve scroll position) but never preserves form state, so any dismissible thing sitting on top of a filled form must be an overlay.

MOBILE NOTE: a bottom sheet is an overlay positioned Bottom centre with a scrim, an On drag Down interaction to dismiss, and Close when clicking outside enabled. A full-screen mobile modal is usually better as Navigate to with a Move in / Bottom transition, because it genuinely replaces the screen.

title: Scroll and Overflow Behaviour
content:
A frame scrolls only when (a) its content extends beyond its bounds and (b) an overflow direction is set. Both conditions are required — this is the most common 'why won't my prototype scroll' bug.

OVERFLOW OPTIONS (Prototype tab → Overflow):
- No scrolling — content is clipped, nothing moves.
- Horizontal — for carousels, chip rows, category rails, token lists.
- Vertical — the default for page bodies.
- Both directions — for canvases, maps, large tables, trading charts.

REQUIREMENTS AND GOTCHAS:
- 'Clip content' does not need to be on for scrolling to work in the prototype, but leave it on so the canvas matches the prototype.
- Content must exceed the frame in the scroll axis. In an auto-layout frame with Hug contents, the frame grows with content and therefore never overflows — set a Fixed height (vertical) or Fixed width (horizontal) on the scrolling frame.
- Nested scroll frames work, and they are how you build a vertically scrolling page containing horizontally scrolling rails. Keep nesting to two levels; deeper nesting becomes unpredictable for the user and hard to test.
- Horizontal scroll on desktop needs an affordance — a partially visible next card, arrows, or a scrollbar. A perfectly aligned row of cards that happens to scroll is undiscoverable.
source: help.figma.com — Prototype scroll and overflow behavior

title: Scroll With Parent, Fixed, and Sticky
content:
Any object inside a scrolling frame has a Position setting in the Prototype tab.

- SCROLL WITH PARENT — default. The object moves with the content.
- FIXED — the object is pinned to the frame's viewport and never moves. Use for headers, bottom tab bars, floating action buttons, persistent 'Add to cart' bars, and the scrim/close button of an overlay.
- STICKY — the object scrolls with the content until it reaches its resting edge, then pins. Use for section headers in long lists, table header rows, sticky category filters, and sticky product-summary bars.

RULES:
- Fixed and Sticky only apply to direct children of the scrolling frame. If your header is nested inside another frame, the setting is unavailable — pull it out to be a direct child.
- A Fixed element must sit ABOVE the scrolling content in layer order or content will render over it.
- Fixed elements do NOT smart-animate when they match across frames; Figma applies no transition to matching fixed layers, and dissolves non-matching ones. If you need a header to animate (shrinking on scroll, for example), that is a Figma Motion or code job, not a Fixed layer.
- Sticky is what makes a long Shopify collection page feel real: sticky filter bar plus a fixed mobile 'Filter / Sort' bar reproduces the actual scroll experience testers will encounter.
source: help.figma.com — Prototype scroll and overflow behavior

title: Preserve Scroll Position — And When It Lies
content:
PRESERVE SCROLL POSITION is a checkbox on a Navigate to interaction. When enabled, the destination frame opens at the same scroll offset the current frame was at.

REQUIREMENTS: source and destination frames must have the same dimensions and the same scrollable content height for the offset to land somewhere sensible.

WHAT IT'S FOR: state changes on a long page. A user 2000px down a collection page taps a filter chip; you Navigate to a variant of the page with the filter applied and Preserve scroll position keeps them where they were. Without it, they are thrown to the top and the prototype reads as broken.

RESET SCROLL POSITION is the inverse and is the correct choice when the destination is a genuinely new page.

WHERE IT LIES: preserving scroll makes a Navigate to feel like an in-place update, but production behaves that way only if the change is client-side. If the real implementation is a page reload — a Shopify collection filter without JS-driven filtering, for instance — your prototype is promising something the build will not deliver. Note the assumption in your handoff, or prototype it honestly with a loading state.

DEEPER LIMITATION: nothing preserves form input, dropdown selection, or component state across a Navigate to unless you have bound it to a variable. If a tester fills three fields, navigates, and comes back to an empty form, that is Figma, not your design. Use overlays or variables for anything stateful.
source: help.figma.com — Preserve scroll position in prototypes

title: Scroll To — In-Page Navigation
content:
Scroll to scrolls the current frame so a specified object comes into view. It does not change frames and does not enter prototype history.

SETTINGS: target object, plus Instant or an animated option with easing and duration.

USE FOR: anchor navigation on a long landing page, 'Jump to reviews' on a product page, in-page tabs on a marketing site, table-of-contents links, 'Back to top', stepper navigation inside one long form.

CRAFT NOTES:
- Animate rather than jump — 400–600ms with ease-in-out reads as 'the page moved', while Instant reads as 'the page changed', which is a different and usually wrong message.
- Longer distances need slightly longer durations, but cap at ~800ms. Beyond that the user has already stopped watching.
- Give the target a visible landing offset. Scrolling a section heading flush to the top edge, under a fixed header, hides it. Add a spacer or target the container rather than the heading.
- Scroll to is the correct prototype for `scroll-behavior: smooth` plus `scroll-margin-top` in CSS. Say so in your handoff note — the offset problem is the same in both places.

title: Prototype Device, Orientation, and Background
content:
Prototype tab, with nothing selected → device settings for the page.

DEVICE: pick a preset (iPhone, Android, tablet, desktop, watch, custom) or None. The choice draws a device chrome around your frames in Presentation view and sets the viewport size.

MODEL AND COLOUR: cosmetic. Choose a device matching your primary user's hardware — showing a Shopify mobile flow inside a Pixel frame when 70% of traffic is iOS Safari subtly misleads the room.

ORIENTATION: portrait or landscape.

BACKGROUND: the colour behind your frames in Presentation view. Set it to a neutral that does not compete with the design. Pure white behind a white UI erases the frame edge and hides the fact that your layout has no page background; a mid-grey or the actual site background colour is more honest.

FIT / SCALING: Presentation view scaling options control whether frames scale to fit, scale down, or show at actual size. For a desktop web prototype, set the frame width to a real breakpoint (1440, 1280) and use 'Fit to screen' — then say explicitly which breakpoint you designed, because a scaled 1440 frame on a 13-inch laptop looks fine and the real thing does not.

DEVICE ≠ VIEWPORT TRUTH. iOS Safari's dynamic toolbar, Android's varying navigation bars, and browser chrome all steal vertical space that Figma's device frame does not model. Design your above-the-fold assuming ~100–150px less height than the frame suggests.
source: help.figma.com — Set prototype device and background settings

title: Presentation View and Sharing Prototypes
content:
Presentation view (Shift+Cmd/Ctrl+Enter, or the Play button) runs the prototype. Anyone with View access can play it; only Edit access can build it.

OPTIONS WORTH SETTING BEFORE YOU SHARE:
- Flow selector — shows all starting points. Name them well; this is the menu stakeholders see.
- 'Show hotspot hints on click' — flashes available hotspots when the user clicks dead space. Turn ON for stakeholder demos and unmoderated tests where a stuck user ends the session. Turn OFF for moderated discoverability testing, where finding the hotspot is the thing you are measuring.
- Zoom / fit options and 'Fill screen'.
- Comments — viewers can leave comments pinned to a point in the prototype.

SHARING:
- Copy the prototype link, not the file link. The prototype link opens straight into Presentation view at the chosen flow.
- 'Anyone with the link can view' for external stakeholders; keep it restricted for anything under NDA or unreleased pricing.
- Figma Mirror shows the prototype on a real device over the network — essential before you trust any mobile touch-target or thumb-zone judgement.

WHAT VIEWERS SEE THAT YOU FORGET: missing custom fonts fall back to Inter for viewers who lack them, and font substitution during a variant Change to can shift layout. For shared prototypes, prefer Google Fonts or confirm the recipient has the font.

title: Video and Audio in Prototypes
content:
Figma supports video fills on frames and shapes, and a set of prototype triggers and actions around them.

TRIGGERS: When video hits (timestamp — past the length fires at the end), When video ends.
ACTIONS: Play / pause video (play, pause, or toggle), Mute / unmute video (mute, unmute, or toggle), Set to specific time, Jump forward / backward in time by N seconds.

USE CASES: an onboarding walkthrough that advances when the clip ends; a product page hero video with a real mute control; a video player UI where scrub, skip, and mute actually work; an autoplay-with-sound-off pattern you can put in front of a legal reviewer.

CRAFT NOTES:
- Video fills inflate file size fast. Keep prototype clips short and compressed; a 40MB hero video will make the file crawl for everyone on the team.
- Prototype the muted-autoplay reality of the mobile web. Browsers block autoplay with sound; a prototype that plays audio on load tests an experience that cannot ship.
- Video does not Smart animate. A frame transition involving a video falls back to dissolve.
- For Shopify product pages: video-as-first-media changes perceived load and LCP. Prototype the poster frame and the transition into playback, and flag the performance cost in handoff.

title: Animated GIFs and Imported Motion
content:
Figma plays animated GIFs in Presentation view. On canvas they show a single frame; in the prototype they loop.

USE FOR: a loading spinner or skeleton shimmer you cannot build with Smart animate; a Lottie animation exported to GIF for a success state; an illustrated empty state with motion; a micro-animation you have received from a motion designer and only need to place.

LIMITS AND HONESTY:
- GIFs always loop and cannot be stopped, started, or timed by a prototype action. A 'success' checkmark GIF will loop forever, which is wrong. Overlay it briefly and swap it out, or accept the inaccuracy and say so.
- GIF has no alpha channel worth using and dithers gradients badly. On a coloured or dark background the fringing is visible.
- File weight is significant. Several GIFs will slow the file.
- Lottie is not natively supported; use a plugin to preview, or export to GIF/MP4 for the prototype and hand the .json to engineering separately.

WHEN TO STOP: if the animation is the thing under review, do not fake it with a GIF. Build it in Figma Motion, where the timeline is inspectable in Dev Mode and exportable as CSS or motion.dev code, or prototype it in code.

title: Prototype Performance — Keeping It Playable
content:
Slow prototypes fail usability tests for reasons that have nothing to do with your design.

WHAT COSTS THE MOST:
- Raster images at full resolution. A 4000px product photo scaled to 320px still loads 4000px. Downsample before importing.
- Video fills. Seconds of compressed video is fine; a minute of 1080p is not.
- Frame count. Hundreds of near-duplicate frames representing state is the classic symptom of not using variables or interactive components.
- Deeply nested component instances, especially instances of instances of instances, each with overrides.
- Blur effects, especially background blur, and many layered shadows — these are re-rendered every frame during a transition.
- Long Smart animate transitions across frames with hundreds of matching layers.

FIXES IN ORDER OF LEVERAGE:
1. Replace duplicated-frame state with variables and interactive components. This routinely cuts frame count by an order of magnitude.
2. Split the file. One file per flow or per surface; libraries stay separate from prototypes.
3. Compress and resize images. Aim for 2x the displayed size, no more.
4. Flatten decorative vector art that will never be edited.
5. Reduce blur and shadow layers on any frame involved in a transition.

BEFORE ANY TEST SESSION: play the whole flow on the actual test machine, over the actual network. First playthrough is always the slowest because assets are still loading — warm it up before the participant arrives.

title: Hotspot Craft — Size, Invisibility, and Placement
content:
A hotspot is any layer carrying an interaction. Its bounds are its hit area, and that has consequences.

SIZE: match the hotspot to the real touch target, not to the visible glyph. A 16px icon needs a 44x44 (iOS) or 48x48 (Android) transparent parent frame carrying the interaction. If you attach the interaction to the 16px icon itself, your prototype tests a target you will never ship — and testers will miss it, giving you a false signal.

INVISIBLE HOTSPOTS: a transparent rectangle over an area is a legitimate shortcut for wiring an un-built region. It is also how prototypes lie. If a whole card is clickable in the prototype because you laid a rectangle over it, make sure the spec says the whole card is clickable — otherwise engineering ships a link on the title only.

PLACEMENT: interactions attached to a COMPONENT propagate to every instance, which is what you want for a button's hover state. Interactions attached to an INSTANCE are local overrides, which is what you want for 'this specific button navigates to checkout'. Get this backwards and you will either wire the same interaction 40 times or accidentally send every button in the file to the same screen.

LAYER ORDER: the topmost layer wins the click. An invisible rectangle above your buttons will swallow every interaction beneath it — the single most common 'my prototype doesn't work' cause.

NAMING: name hotspots for what they do ('btn / add-to-cart'), not what they are ('Rectangle 47'). Smart animate depends on names, and so does anyone reading your file.

title: Connection Hygiene and Prototype Maintenance
content:
A prototype rots faster than a design file because connections are invisible until you open the Prototype tab.

HYGIENE RULES:
- Review connections as a set. Prototype tab shows all connections on the page; scan for lines going nowhere useful, crossing the whole canvas, or bunching on one frame.
- Delete orphans. When you delete a destination frame, the connection dies silently; the hotspot stays and does nothing.
- Keep frames in reading order left-to-right, top-to-bottom on the canvas so connection lines run short and forward. Long backwards-crossing lines are a reliable sign the flow itself is confused.
- One purpose per frame. A frame doing double duty in two flows will eventually need contradictory interactions.
- Hover a layer in the Prototype tab to preview which layers Smart animate considers matching — use this before debugging a transition by trial and error.

VERSIONING: name a version in file history before any significant prototype rework ('v3 — pre-checkout-restructure'). Prototype changes are hard to diff visually and impossible to undo selectively after a session of edits.

WHEN TO REBUILD RATHER THAN REPAIR: if you cannot explain the flow from the connection lines in under a minute, rebuild it. A prototype that only its author can navigate has already failed its purpose.

title: Prototype Fidelity — Match the Build to the Question
content:
Fidelity is not a quality level, it is a choice about which question you are answering. Building higher fidelity than your question needs is the most common waste in design work.

PAPER / SKETCH — answers 'is the flow right?' and 'what are the steps?'. Minutes to build, free to discard. Do this before touching Figma.

GREY-BOX CLICKTHROUGH (frames, Navigate to, Instant) — answers 'can people find it?' and 'does the information architecture hold?'. Hours. Deliberately ugly so feedback stays structural. This is where click tests and first-click tests belong.

STYLED CLICKTHROUGH (real components, real copy, Smart animate) — answers 'does this read as trustworthy / premium / simple?' and 'is the hierarchy right?'. Days. This is the standard stakeholder-review artefact.

STATEFUL PROTOTYPE (variables, conditionals, interactive components) — answers 'does the logic work?', 'what happens on error?', 'does the empty→filled→error progression make sense?'. Days to a week. Required for forms, validation, multi-select, carts, and anything with a counter.

MOTION PROTOTYPE (Figma Motion, or code) — answers 'does this feel right?'. Only Figma Motion or real code answers this; a 300ms Smart animate approximates but does not settle a spring question.

CODE PROTOTYPE — answers 'is it technically feasible?', 'how does it perform on a real device?', 'does it work with real data?'. Reach for it when the risk is technical or data-shaped.

THE DISCIPLINE: write the question down before you build. If you cannot state it in one sentence, you are decorating, not prototyping.

title: Prototype the Riskiest Assumption First
content:
A prototype is an instrument for reducing uncertainty, so build only the part that is uncertain.

METHOD:
1. List the assumptions your design rests on. Be specific: 'users will connect a wallet before seeing prices', 'shoppers understand that the size selector filters availability', 'the AI's suggestion will be trusted enough to accept without editing'.
2. Score each by (a) how badly the design breaks if it is false and (b) how little evidence you have. High/high is your riskiest assumption.
3. Prototype the smallest artefact that tests it. Often a single screen and two states, not a flow.
4. Test, learn, discard the prototype.

WHAT THIS RULES OUT: prototyping the happy path in full fidelity. The happy path is almost never the risk. The risk is the empty state, the error, the slow network, the second-time user, the edge case where inventory is 1, the moment the wallet rejects the signature, the response where the model is wrong.

DOMAIN EXAMPLES:
- Shopify: the risk is rarely the PDP layout; it is whether the variant/availability logic is comprehensible and whether the checkout hand-off loses people.
- Crypto: the risk is the signing moment, the gas estimate, and the irreversible-action confirmation — not the dashboard.
- AI: the risk is what happens when the model is wrong, slow, or refuses — not the empty prompt box.

BUILD TO THROW AWAY. A prototype you are reluctant to delete has become a deliverable, and deliverables stop answering questions.

title: Prototypes in Usability Testing — What Breaks
content:
Figma prototypes are the standard testing instrument and they distort results in predictable ways. Know the distortions.

WHAT BREAKS:
- Free typing. Text input does not accept arbitrary text unless you bind a variable to it; participants type and nothing appears. Either build variable-backed input for the fields that matter or tell the participant the field is pre-filled.
- Form state across navigation. Nothing persists across Navigate to without variables. Participants notice.
- Scroll expectation. Testers scroll further and faster than you built. Extend content below the fold or they will hit a hard stop and conclude the page is empty.
- Dead ends. Every unbuilt tap is a moment of participant self-doubt. Either wire a plausible fallback or say up front 'not everything is clickable'.
- Hover-revealed actions. Invisible on touch, and on desktop they change what participants can discover.
- Latency. Instant transitions everywhere make the product feel faster than it will be. If you are testing perceived performance, build the loading states with After delay.

PROTOCOL CHOICES:
- Turn hotspot hints OFF when measuring discoverability; ON for unmoderated tests where a stuck participant just abandons.
- Give the task, not the route. 'Buy a blue medium shirt', not 'click the blue swatch'.
- Test on the real device with Figma Mirror when touch targets, thumb reach, or one-handed use are in question.
- Record what participants tried and could not do — the unwired taps are data about expectation.

title: Prototype Anti-Patterns
content:
ONE GIANT FLOW. Every screen in the file wired into one starting point. Nobody can navigate it; no question gets answered. Fix: one flow per task.

DUPLICATED FRAMES AS STATE. Twelve near-identical frames for twelve filter combinations. Fix: variables and interactive components.

NAVIGATE TO FOR IN-COMPONENT STATE. A separate frame for the hover state of a button. Fix: Change to.

STACKED OPEN OVERLAYS. Three overlays deep with three scrims. Fix: Swap overlay.

HOTSPOT ON THE GLYPH. Interaction attached to a 16px icon instead of a 44px target. Fix: transparent parent frame at the real target size.

WHILE HOVERING EVERYWHERE. Uncontrollable revert, no exit animation. Fix: Mouse enter + Mouse leave.

INSTANT EVERYTHING. Every transition set to Instant because it was the default. The prototype has no sense of spatial continuity and reads as a slideshow. Fix: choose a transition per relationship (see the transitions module).

SMART ANIMATE AS A DEFAULT. Applied to every connection regardless of whether layers match. Falls back to dissolve silently and you never notice. Fix: check matching layers in the Prototype tab.

HAPPY PATH ONLY. No empty state, no error, no loading, no long-content case. Fix: prototype the four states of every screen — empty, loading, ideal, error — plus the overflow case.

PROTOTYPE AS SPEC. Handing engineering a prototype link and calling it handoff. The prototype shows intent, not values. Fix: Dev Mode annotations, motion specs, and stated assumptions.

title: Accessibility in Prototypes — What You Can and Cannot Test
content:
WHAT FIGMA PROTOTYPES CAN SHOW:
- Visible focus states, if you build them as variants and wire Keyboard triggers to step through them. Tedious but it makes focus order visible and reviewable.
- Touch target sizes, tested on a real device via Figma Mirror.
- Colour contrast of every state, including hover, disabled, and error — states that are routinely designed and never contrast-checked.
- Error recovery flows, including whether an error message is adjacent to its field and whether it survives a navigation.
- Motion intensity, which a reviewer can judge in Presentation view.

WHAT THEY CANNOT SHOW:
- Screen reader output. There is no accessibility tree. Names, roles, and states must be specified in Dev Mode annotations, not implied by the prototype.
- Real tab order. Figma has none; a Keyboard-trigger simulation is a drawing of your intent, not a test of it.
- prefers-reduced-motion. Figma has no reduced-motion mode. You must specify the reduced variant separately.
- Zoom and text scaling behaviour up to 200%.
- Assistive tech interaction with live regions, so no test of whether a toast or validation message is announced.

THEREFORE: pair every prototype with annotations. For each interactive element state the accessible name, the role, the state changes, the focus behaviour, and the reduced-motion fallback. A beautiful prototype with no annotations ships an inaccessible build.

title: Handing Off a Prototype — What Engineers Actually Need
content:
A prototype link is not a spec. It shows intent and hides values.

WHAT TO ADD:
1. INTERACTION TABLE. For each interactive element: trigger, action, destination or state change, and the production equivalent (route change, component prop, API call, client-side state).
2. MOTION SPEC. Duration in ms, easing (named token or exact cubic-bezier / spring parameters), which properties animate, stagger delays, and the reduced-motion fallback. 'Like the prototype' is not a spec — a Figma spring and a CSS spring are not the same maths.
3. STATE INVENTORY. Every state you designed: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, empty, error, success, plus the long-content and zero-item cases.
4. CONDITIONAL LOGIC. If you used Conditional actions, write out the boolean rules in plain language. The prototype's if/else is your business logic and it will otherwise be reverse-engineered from the connections.
5. ASSUMPTIONS AND LIES. Say where the prototype is faster, smarter, or more stateful than the build will be. 'Preserve scroll position assumes client-side filtering.' 'The AI response appears in 400ms; real p50 is 2s — see the loading state.'
6. DEV MODE. Use annotations for spacing, tokens, and behaviour; use the Motion tab in Dev Mode for animation values, which developers can copy as CSS, JSON, or motion.dev code.

FOR SHOPIFY specifically, map each prototyped state to what it costs: a native section setting, Liquid work, or custom JS. A prototyped instant filter may be a significant build.

title: Interactions in Library Components
content:
Interactions attached to a MAIN COMPONENT travel with it — to every instance in the file and to every file consuming the library.

WHAT THIS UNLOCKS: build the interaction once at the source and every consumer gets a working, stateful component. A button whose hover, press, and focus states are wired in the library means nobody ever prototypes a button state again. Same for checkboxes, toggles, accordions, tabs, dropdowns, tooltips, and steppers.

RULES:
- Wire GENERIC state inside the component (hover, pressed, checked, expanded, focus). These are always the same everywhere.
- Wire SPECIFIC destinations on the instance (this button navigates to checkout). These differ per use.
- Edit variant interactions at the source component, not on an instance. Instance-level variant overrides are not reflected in Presentation view.
- 'Reset component state' on an interaction stops a component's last-used variant from persisting across frames. Interactive component state is memorised by default and shared between matching components, which is usually what you want for a nav tab and never what you want for a form that should start empty.
- Font substitution caveat: if a variant change involves font weight or decoration and the viewer lacks the font, Figma may substitute Inter and the layout shifts. Prefer Google Fonts for widely shared prototypes.

GOVERNANCE: publish library updates deliberately. A change to a button's variant interactions propagates into every consumer's prototype, including ones being tested tomorrow.
source: help.figma.com — Create interactive components with variants

title: Prototype QA Checklist — Before You Share It
content:
FLOW
- Every flow has a name and a task-shaped description.
- Playing each flow from its starting point reaches a genuine end state.
- No dead taps on primary paths; secondary dead taps are acknowledged to the audience.
- Back works everywhere it appears, or the back affordance is removed.

STATE
- Empty, loading, ideal, error, and long-content states exist for every screen under review.
- Form state survives whatever navigation the flow requires (variables where needed).
- Interactive components do not leak state between frames unless intended ('Reset component state').

MOTION
- No connection left on the default transition by accident.
- Smart animate connections actually have matching layers — verified by hovering in the Prototype tab, not assumed.
- Durations are deliberate: nothing over ~500ms unless it is doing narrative work.
- Reduced-motion intent is documented even though Figma cannot show it.

SCROLL
- Overflow is set on every frame with content beyond bounds; scroll frames have a Fixed dimension.
- Fixed and Sticky elements are direct children and above the content in layer order.
- Content extends far enough below the fold that testers cannot hit a hard stop.

PRESENTATION
- Correct device, orientation, and a background that does not erase the frame edge.
- Hotspot hints set intentionally for this audience.
- Played once end-to-end on the machine and network you will demo from.
- Fonts available to the recipient, or Google Fonts used.

title: When to Stop Prototyping in Figma
content:
Figma prototyping has a ceiling. Recognising it saves days.

LEAVE FIGMA WHEN:
- The question is about FEEL at the level of spring physics, gesture-following, or interruption. Figma Motion narrows this gap considerably, but drag-following-finger with momentum and rubber-banding is a code question.
- The question involves REAL DATA — long product titles, 400-row tables, empty search results from an actual index, live prices, a real model response. Fake data hides the failure modes you are looking for.
- The question is PERFORMANCE. Perceived speed, jank on a mid-range Android, image loading order, layout shift. Figma renders nothing the way a browser does.
- The interaction is CONTINUOUS AND MULTI-VARIABLE — a canvas, a chart with brushing, a map, a drag-and-drop board with reordering.
- The logic exceeds a handful of variables. Figma's expressions do arithmetic, string concatenation, and boolean comparison. There are no arrays, loops, functions, or persistence. Past a certain point, wiring conditionals is slower than writing the component.
- You are on the third rebuild of the same prototype. That is a signal the medium is wrong.

WHAT TO REACH FOR: an HTML/CSS/JS sketch for feel and data; a React sandbox with your real component library for anything system-shaped; Figma Motion for a motion spec that must be inspectable and exportable; a Wizard-of-Oz setup for AI features where the model's behaviour is the unknown.

STAY IN FIGMA for flow, structure, hierarchy, copy, state inventory, and stakeholder alignment. That is most of the work most of the time.

title: Prototypes for Stakeholders vs Prototypes for Testing
content:
These are different artefacts and conflating them wastes both.

STAKEHOLDER PROTOTYPE — the goal is a decision. Optimise for legibility and momentum.
- Linear. One obvious path, no branches, no dead ends.
- Hotspot hints ON. A stuck executive stops watching.
- Fully styled with real copy and plausible data. Lorem ipsum invites copy feedback instead of the decision you need.
- Include the two or three states that carry the argument (the error you are designing away, the empty state you are fixing) and nothing else.
- Narrate. The prototype supports your framing; it does not replace it.

TESTING PROTOTYPE — the goal is behaviour. Optimise for honesty.
- Branching, with plausible wrong turns wired so a participant's mistake produces a real experience, not a dead end.
- Hotspot hints OFF.
- Realistic content, including the ugly cases — long titles, out-of-stock variants, a rejected transaction, a wrong AI answer.
- Latency where latency will exist.
- No narration at all.

THE CONFLATION FAILURE: showing a testing prototype to executives produces feedback about polish. Showing a stakeholder prototype to participants produces false confidence, because every path works and hints tell them where to click. Build the cheaper one first and keep them as separate flows in the same file.
